iut_type: Set-top box (STB) using a chip/module-level certified Bluetooth stack (Panasonic Connect)
customer_question: Our stack (certified by either the chip vendor or module vendor) supports 20 profiles, but we only use 8 and want to cap/disable the remaining 12. Does capping those unused but already-certified profiles count as modifying the originally certified configuration, requiring full re-certification or at least partial re-testing?
question_variants: Does disabling already-certified profiles we don't use require re-certification of the stack?
Will capping 12 of 20 already-certified profiles trigger partial retesting?
actual_issue: The customer was concerned that disabling unused profiles on a chip/module stack that came pre-certified for all 20 profiles might be treated as altering the certified configuration, forcing unnecessary re-testing.
plain_english_explanation: Capping or disabling profiles that are not going to be used does not require re-testing those capped profiles, as long as those profiles were already certified at the chip or module level. The original chip/module-level certification for those 12 unused profiles remains valid; disabling them at the product level doesn't change the testing requirement, since this isn't treated as a modification of the certified stack itself.
consultant_answer: No — capping profiles that are already certified at the chip or module level does not require retesting those capped profiles, even though you're only actively using 8 of the 20 supported profiles.
decision_logic: Disabling/capping an already-certified profile at the product level is not treated as a modification to the underlying certified stack, so it does not trigger a re-certification or retest obligation for that profile.
final_recommendation: When customers ask whether disabling unused but pre-certified profiles affects their certification status, clarify that capping doesn't equal modifying the certified stack, and no retest is required for the capped profiles.
risk_if_done_wrong: Unnecessarily re-testing already-certified, simply-unused profiles would waste cost and schedule for no compliance benefit; conversely, failing to confirm this rule could leave a customer mistakenly believing their entire stack needs re-certification whenever they disable any subset of features.
